newsitem.title: IRAN: Iranians vote in parliamentary by-elections.
newsitem.headline: Iranians vote in parliamentary by-elections.

text.p: Iranians voted on Friday in parliamentary by-elections to fill 22 seats in the 270-member Majlis, the official IRNA news agency said.
"The parliamentary by-elections started at 15 constituencies from 8.00 a.m. (0430 GMT) on Friday," IRNA said.

It said more than 3,000 polling booths were set up in cities and villages for voters to choose their representatives from among 181 nominees. Voting would go on for 10 hours. First results are expected on Saturday night.

Results from last year's parliamentary polls in Iran's third largest city Isfahan and some other districts were annulled by the Guardian Council, a body of clerics and lawyers which oversees elections, because of alleged irregularities.

Local issues dominated the by-elections campaigns, but there has been tension between conservatives and centrist backers of President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani over a screening process which decides who was allowed to run.
Screening committees set up by the Guardian Council approved 215 candidates from about twice as many contenders last month. Some of the candidates have since withdrawn, newspapers said.

Some political figures and newspapers criticised the annulments of last year's poll results, particularly the one in Isfahan, saying they favoured conservatives who oppose Rafsanjani's reform policies and his centrist supporters.

The conservatives, led by parliamentary speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, maintained their Majlis majority in last year's elections. But analysts said they faced a strong minority coalition of pro-Rafsanjani centrists, radical Islamist intellectuals and labour groups.
The 22 new Majlis members' votes could be significant because of the small gap between parliament's two political blocs, analysts said.
Also at stake is momentum in advance of presidential polls, due to be held in May or June, in which Rafsanjani is barred from running after serving two four-year terms.
Nateq-Nouri appears to be the leading candidate for the post after keeping a high media profile in the past months.
The Guardian Council screens candidates for their belief in Islam and Iran's system of Islamic government, including the rule that the state is headed by a supreme spiritual leader.
Campaigning, allowed for one week up to Wednesday night, was low-key compared to last year's main poll.
But residents in Isfahan, 300 km (185 miles) south of Tehran, said walls were covered with posters and there were cases of rivals tearing up each other's flyers.
